guide.title: Because I could not stop for Death — a guided reading and memorisation plan
guide.description: An unhurried reading of Emily Dickinson’s poem, with short passages, images, sound and gentle returns to the text.

metadata.chunkingStrategy: Passages within original stanzas; chunks of at most two lines. Read aloud and recall at your own pace, without scored exercises.

poem.title: Because I could not stop for Death
poem.author: Emily Dickinson
poem.text:
Because I could not stop for Death –
He kindly stopped for me –
The Carriage held but just Ourselves –
And Immortality.

We slowly drove – He knew no haste
And I had put away
My labor and my leisure too,
For His Civility –

We passed the School, where Children strove
At Recess – in the Ring –
We passed the Fields of Gazing Grain –
We passed the Setting Sun –

Or rather – He passed Us –
The Dews drew quivering and Chill –
For only Gossamer, my Gown –
My Tippet – only Tulle –

We paused before a House that seemed
A Swelling of the Ground –
The Roof was scarcely visible –
The Cornice – in the Ground –

Since then – ’tis Centuries – and yet
Feels shorter than the Day
I first surmised the Horses’ Heads
Were toward Eternity –

metadata.edition: Composition and Literature, printed p. 178, poem 479: six-stanza text, checked against Poetry Foundation poem 47652. Retain en dashes, curly apostrophes and capitals from the anthology; omit its explanatory footnote marker after Tippet. Not the altered twenty-line 1890 text titled The Chariot. Poem is conventionally identified by its first line; year left null rather than confusing composition and publication dates.

sessions.title: A courteous caller
sessions.focusSummary: Meet the passengers and the unhurried voice.

pages.title: An invitation to read
pages.bodyMarkdown: Dickinson imagines Death arriving with the courtesy of a caller. Read the six stanzas aloud and let their familiar journey become gradually strange. The dashes give the voice places to hesitate or turn. You can learn one short stanza at a time, allowing the scenes to remain vivid without deciding exactly what the speaker believes.

pages.title: A courteous caller
pages.bodyMarkdown: The opening sounds almost like an explanation for missing an appointment. Death becomes someone who can stop a carriage, while Immortality appears as another presence within it. This is personification: an abstract idea is given the actions of a person. Listen to the courtesy in kindly, and leave space before the final passenger is named. The familiar tone can make the scene feel stranger.

pages.title: Putting things away
pages.bodyMarkdown: Labor and leisure together suggest the ordinary activities of a whole life. Civility means courteous behaviour. The speaker’s explanation is restrained, even though what she puts aside is immense. Speak the stanza without hurrying, and notice the contrast between the long first line and the brief second one. For memory, follow the drive, the putting away, and the explanation offered for it.

pages.title: Scenes passing
pages.bodyMarkdown: We passed returns as a guide through school, fields and sunset. Strove suggests children busily exerting themselves; recess and the ring place them at play. The scenes can suggest stages of a life, though they remain particular sights beside a road. Notice that the grain seems to gaze back. Hold each view separately, then let the repeated phrase carry you onward.

sessions.focusSummary: Hear the correction and feel the speaker’s thin clothing.

pages.title: A change in the air
pages.bodyMarkdown: Or rather revises the previous stanza: now the sun is passing them. The temperature changes as the dew arrives. Gossamer suggests something extremely fine and light; a tippet is a shoulder covering, and tulle a fine net fabric. The delicate clothing makes the cold bodily and immediate. Give the correction a small pause, then let the repeated light sounds of the clothing meet the chill.

sessions.title: A low house
sessions.focusSummary: Notice the hesitation between naming and seeing.

pages.title: A low house
pages.bodyMarkdown: The speaker calls the stopping place a House, then qualifies what she sees. Its swelling ground and barely visible roof invite us to recognise a grave without being given that word. A cornice is a projecting architectural edge near a roof. Keep the apparent house and the earth together in your mind. The repeated Ground gives the stanza an unusually firm, low resting place.

sessions.title: Centuries and a day
sessions.focusSummary: Let the final change of scale reshape the ride.

pages.title: Centuries and a day
pages.bodyMarkdown: Surmised means inferred or began to suspect. The speaker looks back across centuries that feel shorter than a day. The ending supplies a direction, but leaves the journey’s destination beyond the picture. Read all six stanzas again, letting the ordinary scenes lead into this altered sense of time. You can give the final dash a little silence without trying to close every uncertainty.

pages.title: Keep the poem near
pages.bodyMarkdown: Let the poem rest for now. A phrase may return later, or you may want to read it aloud again with a different emphasis. Familiarity can grow through small, unhurried returns.
